name: The Sundays
label: Rough Trade
lede: Harriet Wheeler and David Gavurin wrote songs in a boiler room, got a bidding war from their first gig, watched their label go bankrupt under their debut, and after three albums simply stopped putting records out.

hero.by: Hannan, Wheeler, Brindley and Gavurin. Wikipedia

eras.title: A boiler room and one gig
eras.text: Two Bristol University graduates on unemployment benefit, with no real musical background between them, wrote songs in a tiny room of a rented London flat. One show was enough to start a fight among record labels.

years.h: Wheeler and Gavurin meet as students at Bristol University
years.p: She was from Reading, studying English literature; he was from Wembley, studying French and Spanish. They fell in love and moved in together.
years.xp: Wheeler had sung a few gigs with Cruel Shoes, an early version of Jim Jiminee, whose line-up also included Patrick Hannan's brother Nick. Otherwise, Wikipedia says, the couple had no musical background.

years.h: Two more Bristol graduates make it a band
years.p: Bassist [[Paul Brindley|7b69cc6a-f72f-4153-ac56-c2ee027045ba]] and drummer Patrick Hannan join. "The Sundays" was the one name all four could agree on.
years.xp: Almost every song for the first album came out of what Classic Pop calls a "minuscule boiler room" in their rented flat. Brindley was never credited as a co-writer.

years.h: Three critics come for the headliner and write about the opener
years.p: A club gives the band an opening slot off their demo tape. "By chance there were three reviewers from the top music papers there," Wheeler said.
years.xp:
Melody Maker's Chris Roberts called them "the best thing I've ever heard", according to Classic Pop. A bidding war followed. 4AD's [[Ivo Watts-Russell|cf86cec1-1baf-4d8a-ba1e-01568332585a]] was in front for a while, but they picked [[Rough Trade|4f4b0013-1704-4936-a769-e6e8a6e08ff8]], partly, Gavurin said, because it was near their flat.

"They seemed incredibly straightforward," Gavurin said of Rough Trade's [[Geoff Travis|70437714-3183-4916-947f-e5ba2154d16a]] and Jeannette Lee. DGC took them in the US.

eras.title: Here's where the story starts
eras.text: Rough Trade took more than a year to get an album out of a band that wrote slowly and threw nothing away. When it came, it went top five in Britain, gold in America, and onto college radio for good.

years.h: "Can't Be Sure" tops the indie chart
years.p: The debut single, backed with "I Kicked a Boy", reaches No. 45 on the national chart, and in December wins John Peel's Festive 50 listeners' poll.

years.src: uDiscover · Classic Pop · Wikipedia: The Sundays
years.h: Perfectionists in the studio with Ray Shulman and Alan Moulder
years.p: Ex-Gentle Giant bassist Ray Shulman co-produces the album, with [[Alan Moulder|1b75cdb6-4d61-4ff5-b699-28075b867b4c]] engineering. Jeannette Lee called the band particular, because they wanted to be very certain about what they put out.
years.xp: "We didn't have enough for our first album, let alone our second," Gavurin said. "We can't write to deadline."

yt: MTV news feature with Kurt Loder, 1990
years.h: Reading, Writing and Arithmetic goes to No. 4
years.p: Eighteen months after the first gig, the debut hits the UK top five and No. 39 in the US. Wikipedia puts worldwide sales over half a million.

yt: Here's Where the Story Ends video
years.h: "Here's Where the Story Ends" goes to No. 1 on US Modern Rock
years.p: MTV and college radio carry it across America, and the band spends almost a year touring the US, Europe and Japan.
years.xp:
The tour had its moments. A London show was rescheduled when Wheeler lost her voice, and a Dallas promoter advertised the gig as a chance to see the Sundays on Sunday with ice-cream sundaes.

Lindsay Jamieson joined on tambourine for the road. Wikipedia says the band called the tour exhausting.

eras.title: The label goes under
eras.text: Rough Trade's collapse took the band's home and, in Britain, their first album with it. Managing themselves and writing at their own pace, the Sundays went quiet long enough for the papers to wonder whether they'd split.

years.h: Rough Trade's distribution arm collapses, taking the Sundays' deal
years.p: That's Rough Trade's Jeannette Lee. The band moves to Parlophone in the UK, and Reading, Writing and Arithmetic goes out of print in Britain until 1996.
years.xp:
Gavurin told Classic Pop the band was simply told there was a problem that needed looking at. Rough Trade's distribution company went bankrupt in 1991.

With no manager, the band handled its own business. Combined with slow writing, Wikipedia says, it kept them out of sight, and rumours went round that they'd broken up.

years.cap: Wheeler at Queens Hall, Bradford, c. 1992
years.h: "Goodbye", nearly three years after the last UK show
years.p: The comeback single reaches No. 27. Its B-side is a cover of [[The Rolling Stones|b071f9fa-14b0-4217-8e97-eb41da73f598]]' "Wild Horses".

years.h: Blind, on Parlophone and Geffen
years.p: A darker second album, No. 15 in the UK. "Love" goes to No. 2 on the US Modern Rock chart.
years.xp: Some critics thought the songs fell short of the debut's. The album still went gold in the US, and the British winter tour was, in the words Wikipedia quotes, rapturously received by fans starved of new material.

yt: Here's Where the Story Ends, live in Seattle, 1993
years.h: Sold-out American shows, then home early
years.p: The US tour sells out, with half the set from the first album. It's cut short; Wikipedia gives exhaustion and homesickness as the reasons.

eras.title: Thailand, a daughter, horns
eras.text: After a holiday the band put its career on hold. A beer advert and a horror film kept "Wild Horses" in circulation while Wheeler and Gavurin started a family and built a studio at home, and the last album took five years.

years.h: Budweiser borrows "Wild Horses" for an American TV ad
years.p: It's the band's only public appearance of the year. Two years later the cover turns up in the thriller Fear.

years.h: Wheeler and Gavurin's daughter Billie is born
years.p: The couple also build a studio in their house, to save on hire costs and work on their own clock.

years.h: Static & Silence, five years after Blind
years.p: Same sound, plus horns. Reviews were mixed, but it reached No. 10 in the UK.

yt: Summertime, live on Top of the Pops
years.h: "Summertime" becomes the Sundays' biggest UK hit
years.p: No. 15 in Britain and top ten on US alternative radio, eight years after their first single.

years.h: Nine hundred people at Union Chapel see the last show
years.p: The Sundays play the Islington church just before Christmas. It's their last public show to date.
years.xp: Gavurin, looking back that year: "Even before we had a single out, we were on the cover of music magazines. There was quite a lot of pressure."

eras.title: Still writing, maybe
eras.text: The band never announced a split, and everyone close to them says the music didn't stop. None of it has come out.

years.h: An airline magazine editor tracks them down
years.p: American Way's Adam Pitluk asks about a reunion. Their answer: first let's see if the music they're writing now ever sees the light of day.

q: They're the most paranoid people about actually putting stuff out there.
years.h: David Baddiel on his "oldest mate" Gavurin
years.p: On BBC 6 Music, Baddiel says the couple are still making music but are the most paranoid people about putting it out.

years.h: Hannan says he's drummed on their new songs
years.p: On the C86 Show podcast, Patrick Hannan says Wheeler and Gavurin never stopped making music. The recordings may never be released.

years.h: Thirty-five years on, the Independent goes looking
years.p: A feature notes that the band never put their own faces on their sleeves, and that a fan account has been asking where Wheeler is since 2020.
